title: Which One, and the Form the Book Owed You

lessons.title: welcher — "which," and the two pieces inside it
lessons.gloss: which — built as "what-like", the identical two pieces English welded into which

segments.text: Wer asks which person. Was asks which thing. Neither can ask which one of these, and that is the word this lesson buys.

segments.instruction: two chapters back, the three shapes of the negative article — kein, keine, keinen
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: two chapters back, the three shapes of the negative article — *kein*, *keine*, *keinen*]

segments.text: welcher — "which", standing in front of a noun.
The ending copies the article the noun already takes, so you have nothing new to learn once you know its gender: welcher for a der-word, welche for a die-word, welches for a das-word.
Welcher Hund?, Welche Katze?, Welches Brot?
Said VEL-cher, with the soft ich-sound of ich and nicht in the middle.
welcher is two ancient pieces: hwa- — the what you already meet at the front of every W-word — and -lîk, "like, bodily form", the ancestor of English -ly and of the word like itself. What-like.

English built its own word out of the very same two: hwā + līc gave hwilc, which wore down to which. So both languages ask "which one" by asking "what kind", and the shared seam is still visible if you set wel-cher beside wh-ich.
Say the article first, then the matching shape.

segments.instruction: der Hund becomes "Welcher Hund?"
die Katze becomes "Welche Katze?"
das Brot becomes "Welches Brot?"
der Kaffee becomes "Welcher Kaffee?"
die Milch becomes "Welche Milch?"

segments.text: "Welcher Hund? Welche Katze? Welches Brot?"

What decides the ending on welcher? (The article the noun takes.) Give all three. (Welcher, welche, welches.) What two pieces is it built from? (Hwa- and -lîk — "what-like".) Which English word was built the same way? (Which.)

lessons.title: wie viel, wie viele — how much and how many
lessons.gloss: how much and how many — one distinction German marks and English marks too, on a word that is English full

segments.text: You can count to twenty and you cannot ask anybody for a number. Say zwölf and zwanzig, then take the question that was missing.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: wie viel, wie viele

segments.text: wie viel — "how much", for something you would not count. wie viele — "how many", for things you would.
Wie viel Milch? — how much milk., Wie viele Hunde? — how many dogs.
English draws the identical line with two words too, much against many, so nothing is new except the German for it. The -e on viele is the plural ending you have carried since die.
One phrase to bank whole: Wie viel Uhr ist es?, literally how much clock is it.

viel is Proto-Indo-European pelh₁-, "to fill". Grimm's law turned that p into f, as it did in Fuß against Latin pes, and the word reached English as full. The same root sits in Greek poly- and Latin plenus. German asks how full where English asks how much.
Decide countable or not before you speak.

segments.text: "Wie viel Milch? Wie viele Hunde?"

Which one goes with milk, and why? (Wie viel — milk is not counted.) Which goes with dogs? (Wie viele.) What English word is viel? (Full, by the same p becomes f step that gave Fuß.) Ask the time. (Wie viel Uhr ist es?)

lessons.title: den — the form the book has owed you since einen
lessons.gloss: the — for a der-word that is the thing being done to; the system the einen lesson handed over as a bare word and promised for later

segments.text: Say einen and keinen. Both wear an -en that no other shape of their word wears, and both were handed to you as plain words with the promise that the system behind them would come later. It comes now.
den — "the", for a der-word that is the thing being done to.
Der Hund ist hier. becomes Ich habe den Hund.
The dog standing is der Hund; the dog being had is den Hund. German writes the difference on the article rather than on the noun.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one row of three moves

segments.text: When a noun is the thing being done to, only the der-words change shape.

utterances: naming it: der Hund. doing something to it: den Hund.
naming it: die Milch. doing something to it: die Milch.
naming it: das Brot. doing something to it: das Brot.

segments.text: That is the whole announcement, and it is smaller than German's reputation suggests. Die and das stand still. So do their ein and kein partners — eine, keine, ein, kein — while ein becomes einen and kein becomes keinen on exactly the row where der becomes den.
Three words you already say, all moving together, all on one row. Nothing new has been added; a pattern has been pointed at.

English ran this system too and threw nearly all of it away. Three survivors remain, all pronouns: whom, him, them. "Whom did you see" is precisely what den does. English kept the marking only where it was shortest; German kept it on the article, where it stays visible on every noun.
Name it, then do something to it.

segments.instruction: "der Hund" becomes "Ich habe den Hund."
"der Wein" becomes "Ich habe den Wein."
"der Kaffee" becomes "Ich habe den Kaffee."

segments.text: "Der Hund — den Hund."

Which of the three articles changes when its noun is done to? (Only der, which becomes den.) Which two words you already say change on the same row? (Einen and keinen.) Which three English words are the last survivors of the same system? (Whom, him, them.)

lessons.title: Der Tag ist gut — the adjective that stays still
lessons.gloss: the adjective that does not move — an ending arrives only when the adjective stands in front of its noun

segments.text: Say gut, then guten Tag, then gute Nacht. The same adjective wears three shapes, and you have never been told what decides which.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the ending comes from standing in front

segments.text: A German adjective takes an ending only when it stands in front of its noun. After ist, it stands bare.
Der Tag ist gut. — bare. The adjective comes after the verb.
Guten Tag. — an ending. The adjective comes before the noun.

So the greeting and the verdict are the same word in two positions, and the position is the whole story. This is the single most economical thing in German adjectives: half of all the adjective forms in the language are the dictionary word, unchanged, and you get that half free.
English does the opposite of both halves: it never inflects an adjective at all, in either position. The day is good, good day — one shape, always.
So every German adjective you own is already usable after ist with no work:
Die Katze ist schwarz., Der Wein ist rot., Ich bin müde.
The colours from the colour chapters, the müde from the wellbeing chapter and the gut from page one all behave the same way the moment a verb stands in front of them.

lessons.title: es gibt — "it gives," which is German for "there is"
lessons.gloss: there is, there are — literally "it gives", and it takes the done-to form this chapter has taught

segments.text: You met es as the weather's subject — the es that stands for nobody. It has one more famous job, and it needs the form you learned two lessons ago.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: es gibt

segments.text: es gibt — "there is", "there are". Literally: it gives.
Es gibt Kaffee. — "There is coffee."
Es gibt einen Hund. — "There is a dog."
Es gibt keinen Kaffee. — "There is no coffee."
The phrase never changes shape. Whether one thing exists or twenty, it stays es gibt — the es is the same empty subject as in the weather, standing in a slot German insists on filling.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: what follows it is an object

segments.text: Because geben means give, the thing that exists is grammatically the thing being given — so it takes the done-to form this chapter has taught.
Es gibt den Hund., Es gibt einen Hund., Es gibt keinen Hund.
Every one of those is a der-word wearing its -n, and that is not a special rule for es gibt. It is the ordinary rule, arriving in the commonest sentence you will ever want it in.

Four languages, four different verbs for the same idea: German gives it, French has it there, Spanish has it outright, English puts it there. Only German's choice makes the thing an object, and that is why es gibt is the place a learner meets the case system whether or not anyone explained it.

segments.text: "Es gibt keinen Kaffee."

What does es gibt say word for word? (It gives.) Does it change when there are many things? (No — it never moves.) What form does the thing after it take? (The done-to form — einen, keinen, den.) Say "there is no coffee." (Es gibt keinen Kaffee.)
